storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere nearby this evening — high pressure keeps it dry, quiet and partly cloudy, with nothing on radar.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the 60°F Sound is already about 3°F warmer than the air at 4 PM, and that gap widens to ~6°F the other way by 7 PM as the air cools — the Sound isn't shielding the cove, but there's nothing to shield it from.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: A strong high-pressure system (about 1030 hPa) sits over southern New England. The KOKX radar shows no echoes at all, there are no NWS watches, warnings or advisories, and the HRRR model has zero storm energy (CAPE of 0 J/kg) through the evening. Winds aloft are brisk (about 48 kt of west-southwest shear), but without any instability there is nothing for that wind to organize into storms.

Local modifier: On summer days the cool Long Island Sound often lays a stable marine layer over the cove that weakens incoming storms. That only works when the air is at least ~5°F warmer than the water. Tonight it's the reverse: Sound water is about 60°F while the air is 56–57°F, so the protective gap is already gone at 4 PM. As the air keeps cooling after the 5:54 PM sunset (the Sound holds its temperature while the air drops), the air ends up roughly 6°F colder than the water by 7 PM. There is no sea breeze either — it needs warm land, and today's land–sea contrast is backwards.

Most likely outcome: A dry, quiet evening for the cove and the surrounding towns alike. Partly sunny skies turn mostly cloudy around sunset, then partly cloudy later. Light southeast-to-south breeze.

What would change the call: Nothing in the current data points to a change. A new radar echo moving in from the west, or an NWS advisory, would be the trigger — and with no instability at all, even that would most likely be light showers rather than thunderstorms.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander
wind.tactics_blurb: Drifter conditions in the shadow of Greenwich Point — whatever pressure there is sits on the west (right) side of the course. Work right toward Field Point and expect the breeze to clock slowly from east toward south through the evening.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day: This is a light gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day. A sea breeze needs the land to be at least ~5°F warmer than the water; today the air (about 57°F) is actually about 3°F cooler than the 60°F Sound, so there's no thermal engine at all. The background wind is weak too — airport and buoy anemometers average just 5 kt, with high pressure parked overhead.

Direction and where the pressure is: The breeze is coming from the east to east-southeast (Riverside YC reads ESE 115° at 2.9 kt, gusting 6; the western Sound buoy shows E at 7–8 kt). Easterly winds are the cove's worst direction: Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) sits directly upwind and blankets the start area, so the open Sound can look breezier than the line. Pressure favors the west side of the course, away from the point's shadow — on an upwind leg into an ESE–SE breeze that's the right-hand side.

Through the window: The wind softens around the 5:54 PM sunset, then slowly clocks right — east at 6 PM, southeast by 7 PM, toward south by 9–10 PM — as the high drifts offshore. Each step toward south opens the cove up a little more, but speeds stay in the 2–4 kt range and drop toward drifting by 10 PM. Because the Sound is warmer than the air, the breeze over the water won't go completely dead after dark the way it can on a calm summer night, but don't expect it to build either.

Model check: The HRRR model calls for east-northeast at 6 PM, while stations around the western Sound already show southeast (126°) — about 35° further right. The NWS hourly forecast agrees with the stations (SE, then S). This forecast leans on the station observations and NWS for direction. HRRR data stops at 7 PM this run, so the 8–10 PM hours come from the NWS hourly forecast and carry lower confidence.

What racers will feel: Real drifter conditions — 2–4 kt with puffs to 5–6. Heavier boats will struggle to keep steerage; dinghies will be hunting for every puff. Keep the boat moving over pointing, look for dark water coming off the Sound on the west side, and expect the race committee to think hard about shortening course.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours f05–f12 unavailable — 20:00–22:00 wind hours based on NWS hourly forecast and persistence (lower confidence)
HRRR/observation direction gap of 35° (model E 91°, western-Sound stations SE 126°) — forecast direction leans on observations and NWS
